lesson.title: Two Roads to a New Species: Allopatric and Sympatric Speciation
lesson.summary: Speciation is the process by which one population splits into two reproductively isolated groups, and it comes down largely to geography: allopatric speciation happens when a physical barrier separates populations first, while sympatric speciation happens without any geographic separation at all.
lesson.body:
Speciation is the process by which a single ancestral population becomes two or more populations that meet the biological species concept's core requirement: they can no longer interbreed and produce fertile offspring, even if they later come back into contact. Everything covered earlier in this unit, drift, founder effects, bottlenecks, restricted gene flow, mutation, and the different modes of natural selection, are the actual mechanisms that can push two populations' allele frequencies apart from an initial shared starting point described by Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Speciation is what happens when that divergence goes far enough, for long enough, that reproductive isolation is the result, whether through genetic incompatibilities, behavioral differences, physical mismatches, or some combination of causes that prevent successful interbreeding.

The more common and more straightforward of the two basic geographic modes is allopatric speciation, in which a physical barrier, a mountain range, a river changing course, a land bridge disappearing, or a few individuals colonizing a distant island, first separates a population into two groups that can no longer exchange genes. Once gene flow between the two groups is cut off, whatever other forces are acting, drift especially in a small newly isolated group, along with mutation and natural selection responding to each group's own local environment, are free to push the two populations' allele frequencies apart without gene flow pulling them back together. Given enough time, the two isolated populations can accumulate enough genetic difference that, even if the geographic barrier later disappears and the two groups come back into contact, they can no longer interbreed successfully. A commonly cited example is the Kaibab squirrel and Abert's squirrel, populations of tassel eared squirrels living on opposite rims of the Grand Canyon, isolated from each other by the canyon itself and today recognizable as distinct forms.

Sympatric speciation is the less common and, historically, more debated alternative: reproductive isolation arising between populations that continue to live in the same geographic area, with no physical barrier separating them at all. Because there is no geography doing the initial separating, sympatric speciation requires some other force to interrupt gene flow between subgroups of a single population that remain in contact. Disruptive selection is one route. Recall the finch example from earlier in this unit, where individuals with small and large bills each specialized on a different food resource. If that specialization is paired with a tendency to mate preferentially within one's own phenotype group rather than across the two, gene flow between the two bill size clusters can be reduced even without any geographic separation, potentially setting the two clusters on separate evolutionary trajectories. In plants, sympatric speciation can also happen almost instantly through polyploidy, an error in cell division that leaves offspring with extra complete sets of chromosomes. A polyploid plant is often unable to produce fertile offspring when crossed with its non-polyploid parent population, creating reproductive isolation in a single generation without any geographic separation whatsoever.

In both modes, the underlying test for whether speciation has actually been completed is the same one supplied by the biological species concept: can the two groups still interbreed and produce fertile offspring under natural conditions. Allopatric and sympatric speciation describe two different starting conditions, geographically separated versus geographically overlapping, but the destination in both cases is the same, a level of reproductive isolation sufficient to keep two gene pools permanently apart. This overview only scratches the surface of how that isolation actually gets built, through mechanisms ranging from simple geographic distance to genetic incompatibilities to behavioral mismatches in mate recognition, each of which deserves closer attention in its own right.
